_note: Failure playbooks. Each incident is matched to the first mode of its equipment type whose 'when' conditions all hold on a recent reading ([metric, op, value]; ops < <= > >= == !=). The last mode of each type has no conditions, so a cause is always named. 'reasoning' is filled from the reading ({metric} or {metric:.1f}). Hours and parts cost are planning assumptions for the demo.

modes.title: Worn or slipping fan belt
modes.cause: The belt between the motor and the blower is worn and slipping, so the fan turns slower and moves less air across the cooling coil.
modes.reasoning: Fan speed is {fan_speed_rpm:.0f} rpm (normal about 1,150) while supply air is {temperature_c:.1f} C (setpoint about 24 C). Air temperature rising as the fan slows is the belt-slip pattern; a refrigerant or filter fault would heat the air with the fan at normal speed.
steps: Shift load to the neighbouring CRAC unit or raise its fan speed.
Lock out the unit and check belt tension and wear.
Replace the belt and re-tension to spec.
Run the unit and confirm the fan is back near 1,150 rpm and supply air is at setpoint.

modes.title: Clogged filter or low refrigerant
modes.cause: The fan is moving air normally but the air is not being cooled enough: a clogged air filter or coil, or low refrigerant from a leak.
modes.reasoning: Supply air is {temperature_c:.1f} C with the fan at a normal {fan_speed_rpm:.0f} rpm, so airflow is fine and heat removal is the problem.
steps: Check the filter pressure drop and replace the filter if loaded.
Inspect and clean the coil.
Check suction and discharge pressure; if low, leak-test and recharge.
Confirm supply air returns to setpoint.

modes.title: Cooling drifting off setpoint
modes.cause: Supply air is drifting from its setpoint before any single fault is clear; most often an early filter or belt problem.
modes.reasoning: Supply air {temperature_c:.1f} C, fan {fan_speed_rpm:.0f} rpm: outside the normal band but not yet a full fault pattern.
steps: Check filter, belt tension and refrigerant pressure in that order (cheapest first).
Compare with the neighbouring unit's readings.
Watch the trend for the next hour.

modes.title: Disk surface failing
modes.cause: The platters or flash cells are wearing out; the drive is remapping bad sectors and some data can no longer be read.
modes.reasoning: {reallocated_sectors} sectors remapped, {pending_sectors} pending and {reported_uncorrectable} unreadable. Remapped sectors climbing this fast is the strongest single predictor of drive failure in the Backblaze data the model was trained on.
steps: Confirm the RAID set still has redundancy.
Copy or rebuild the data onto a spare.
Hot-swap the drive.
Let the RAID rebuild finish and verify.

modes.title: Cable or backplane errors
modes.cause: Data is being corrupted on the way to the drive: a loose or damaged cable or a bad backplane slot, not the disk itself.
modes.reasoning: {crc_errors} CRC errors with few media errors points at the connection, not the platters.
steps: Reseat the drive in its slot.
Swap the cable or move the drive to another slot.
Watch CRC errors stop rising.

modes.title: Drive wearing out
modes.cause: Early signs of wear on an ageing drive ({power_on_hours} power-on hours).
modes.reasoning: The failure model scores this drive above normal risk; remapped sectors {reallocated_sectors}, temperature {temperature_c} C.
steps: Check backups and RAID health.
Schedule a replacement in the next maintenance window.

modes.title: Overstrain on a worn tool
modes.cause: The load is more than the worn tool can take: torque times tool wear is past the overstrain limit.
modes.reasoning: Torque {torque_nm:.1f} Nm on a tool with {tool_wear_min} min of wear while speed fell to {rotational_speed_rpm} rpm. In the AI4I data, this torque-times-wear product is what precedes overstrain failures.
steps: Pause the job at a safe point.
Replace the cutting tool.
Reduce feed or load for the next run.
Restart and watch torque.

modes.title: Tool at end of life
modes.cause: The cutting tool has run past its service life.
modes.reasoning: {tool_wear_min} minutes of wear (limit about 200-240).
steps: Replace the tool at the next stop.
Reset the wear counter.

modes.title: Machine under abnormal load
modes.cause: Torque, speed and temperature together look like rising mechanical strain.
modes.reasoning: The AI4I failure model scores this machine at elevated risk: torque {torque_nm} Nm, speed {rotational_speed_rpm} rpm.
steps: Inspect the tool and spindle.
Reduce load until checked.

modes.title: Miner cooling fan failure
modes.cause: A cooling fan has failed, so the chips overheat and throttle.
modes.reasoning: Fan at {fan_speed_rpm} rpm (normal 4,200-5,400) and chips at {chip_temp_c} C.
steps: Underclock the miner to cut heat.
Swap the failed fan (hot-swappable).
Confirm chip temperature drops below 80 C.

modes.title: Hashboard failing
modes.cause: One of the miner's hashboards is failing: hashrate drops and hardware errors rise while the fans and temperature are normal.
modes.reasoning: Hashrate {hashrate_ths} of {rated_hashrate_ths} TH/s with {hw_error_pct}% hardware errors.
steps: Confirm which board is down in the miner's status page.
Move the unit to the repair bench.
Swap the hashboard and re-run.

modes.title: Server crashed
modes.cause: The server stopped answering: an OS or firmware hang, or a hardware fault that took the whole box down.
modes.reasoning: The server is offline with all GPUs gone and power down to {power_w} W, so it is not a single-GPU problem.
steps: Restart the job from its last checkpoint without this server.
Check the BMC event log out-of-band.
Power-cycle the server; if it fails POST, swap the failed board.
Run GPU diagnostics, then return it to the job.

modes.title: GPU dropped off the bus
modes.cause: One GPU failed after its memory errors climbed and the driver lost it.
modes.reasoning: {gpus_online} of 8 GPUs online after ECC errors rose to {ecc_errors}: memory errors climbing and then the GPU vanishing is the classic failing-HBM pattern.
steps: Drain the server from its job (restart from checkpoint).
Confirm the failed GPU in the BMC and driver logs.
Swap the GPU or baseboard.
Run burn-in diagnostics before returning it.

modes.title: GPU memory failing
modes.cause: A GPU's memory is producing correctable errors and running hot; it usually fails within hours.
modes.reasoning: {ecc_errors} ECC errors with the hottest GPU at {max_gpu_temp_c} C.
steps: Plan to drain the server at the next checkpoint.
Swap the GPU before it drops off the bus.

modes.title: Power supply failed
modes.cause: One of the two power supplies failed; the server runs on the other with no redundancy left.
modes.reasoning: {psu_ok} of 2 PSUs healthy while drawing {power_w} W: one more failure takes the server down.
steps: Order or fetch a spare PSU.
Hot-swap the failed PSU (no downtime).
Confirm both PSUs report OK.

modes.title: Throttling from hot inlet air
modes.cause: The rack's inlet air is too warm, so the GPUs throttle; the fix is the cooling unit, not the server.
modes.reasoning: Inlet air {inlet_temp_c} C, {gpus_throttled} GPUs throttling, slowest clock {min_gpu_clock_pct}%.
steps: Find the cooling unit serving this rack and check it.
Check blanking panels and containment doors on this rack.
Confirm GPU clocks recover once inlet air is back below 27 C.

modes.title: UPS battery degraded
modes.cause: Battery cells are ageing or overheating, so the UPS can no longer carry the load long enough for the generator to start.
modes.reasoning: Runtime is {runtime_min:.1f} min at {load_pct:.0f}% load (needs at least 8 min to bridge to the generator), battery at {battery_temp_c:.1f} C.
steps: Confirm the generator is ready to take load.
Run a battery impedance test to find weak strings.
Replace the weak battery strings.
Re-run a runtime test.

modes.title: Running on battery
modes.cause: Utility input was lost or is out of range, so the UPS is carrying the load from its batteries.
modes.reasoning: Input voltage {input_voltage_v:.0f} V and the UPS is on battery at {battery_charge_pct:.0f}% charge.
steps: Check that the generator started and the transfer switch moved.
Check the utility feed and upstream breakers.
Shed non-critical load if runtime is short.

modes.title: UPS overloaded or overheating
modes.cause: The UPS is near its load or temperature limit.
modes.reasoning: Load {load_pct:.0f}%, battery temperature {battery_temp_c:.1f} C.
steps: Move load to the other UPS module.
Check the UPS room cooling.

modes.title: Generator may not start
modes.cause: The generator's starting battery is weak, so it may not crank when the power fails.
modes.reasoning: Start battery at {start_battery_v:.1f} V (healthy 25-27 V).
steps: Charge or replace the starting batteries.
Run a no-load start test.
Schedule the monthly load test.

modes.title: Generator fuel low
modes.cause: Not enough diesel for a long outage.
modes.reasoning: Fuel at {fuel_pct:.0f}% of the tank.
steps: Order a fuel delivery.
Check for leaks at the day tank and lines.

modes.title: Generator mechanical fault
modes.cause: The last test failed or the engine runs hot: injector, coolant or governor fault.
modes.reasoning: Coolant at {coolant_temp_c:.0f} C, last test passed: {last_test_ok}.
steps: Call the generator service contractor.
Arrange a rental generator if the fix takes days.

modes.title: Transfer switch failed to transfer
modes.cause: The automatic transfer switch did not move to the generator when it should, so the load stays on a failing source.
modes.reasoning: Utility at {utility_voltage_v:.0f} V and the switch reports a failed transfer.
steps: Transfer manually under the switching procedure (two-person rule).
Inspect the ATS controller and contacts.
Test the transfer before closing out.

modes.title: Utility power out of range
modes.cause: Utility voltage is out of range; the site is on, or about to move to, generator power.
modes.reasoning: Utility at {utility_voltage_v:.0f} V (nominal 480 V).
steps: Confirm the generator is carrying load.
Contact the utility.

modes.title: Circuit near breaker trip
modes.cause: One phase is drawing close to its breaker rating; one more server spinning up trips the breaker and drops half the rack.
modes.reasoning: Phases at {phase_a_amps:.1f} / {phase_b_amps:.1f} / {phase_c_amps:.1f} A on {breaker_rating_amps} A breakers: the busiest is at {max_phase_pct:.0f}% (code limit 80% continuous).
steps: Move one server's power cord to the least loaded phase.
Cap GPU power on this rack until rebalanced.
Update the rack's power budget.

modes.title: Phase imbalance
modes.cause: Load is spread unevenly across the three phases.
modes.reasoning: Phase imbalance {imbalance_pct:.0f}% (keep under 20%).
steps: Rebalance cords across phases at the next window.

modes.title: Chiller losing capacity
modes.cause: The chiller is not cooling the water enough: a compressor or refrigerant fault, or fouled condenser tubes.
modes.reasoning: Chilled water leaving at {supply_water_c:.1f} C (setpoint 7 C) with the compressor at {compressor_amps:.0f} A.
steps: Start the standby chiller.
Check refrigerant pressures and compressor current.
Clean the condenser if fouled.

modes.title: Low chilled-water flow
modes.cause: Water flow dropped: a pump, valve or strainer problem.
modes.reasoning: Flow {flow_lps:.1f} L/s.
steps: Switch to the standby pump.
Clean the strainer.
Check valve positions.

modes.title: Liquid-cooling leak
modes.cause: Coolant is escaping from a hose, fitting or cold plate in the liquid loop.
modes.reasoning: Leak sensor tripped and loop pressure fell to {pressure_kpa:.0f} kPa.
steps: Isolate the loop branch with the leak valves.
Shut down the servers on that branch safely.
Find and replace the failed fitting or hose.
Refill, bleed air and pressure-test.

modes.title: Coolant pump weak
modes.cause: The CDU pump is not moving enough coolant, so cold plates run hot.
modes.reasoning: Flow {flow_lps:.2f} L/s, coolant supply {coolant_supply_c:.1f} C.
steps: Switch to the redundant pump.
Inspect the failed pump.

modes.title: Water under the raised floor
modes.cause: A pipe, condensate drain or roof leak is putting water under the floor near live power.
modes.reasoning: The under-floor water rope tripped in this hall.
steps: Find the source: CRAC condensate pans and pipes first.
Stop the leak and dry the area.
Check under-floor power whips for damage.

modes.title: Humidity too high (condensation risk)
modes.cause: Air is moist enough to condense on cold surfaces and corrode boards.
modes.reasoning: Relative humidity {humidity_pct:.0f}% (keep 20-60%), dew point {dew_point_c:.1f} C.
steps: Run the CRAC units in dehumidify mode.
Check for open doors or outside air leaks.

modes.title: Air too dry (static risk)
modes.cause: Very dry air lets static build up and discharge into components.
modes.reasoning: Relative humidity {humidity_pct:.0f}% (keep above 20%).
steps: Check the humidifier.
Remind staff to use wrist straps.

modes.title: Failing optic or dirty fibre
modes.cause: Light reaching the receiver is too weak: a dirty connector, a bent fibre or a dying transceiver.
modes.reasoning: Receive power {optic_rx_dbm:.1f} dBm (healthy above -10) with {port_errors_per_min:.0f} errors a minute.
steps: Clean both fibre ends with a one-click cleaner.
Swap the transceiver.
Replace the patch cord if errors continue.

modes.title: Links down
modes.cause: Ports have gone down: a failed line card, cable or a configuration push.
modes.reasoning: {links_down} links down and {packet_loss_pct:.1f}% packet loss.
steps: Check recent configuration changes and roll back if any.
Check the cables and optics on the down ports.
Fail traffic to the redundant switch.

modes.title: Switch overloaded or overheating
modes.cause: The switch's control plane is busy or hot, often from a traffic storm or a failed fan.
modes.reasoning: Switch at {temperature_c:.0f} C with CPU {cpu_pct:.0f}% and {packet_loss_pct:.1f}% loss.
steps: Look for a broadcast storm or DDoS and filter it.
Check the switch fans.
Move traffic to the redundant path.

modes.title: Smoke detected
modes.cause: The air-sampling detector sees smoke: an overheating cable, PSU or battery.
modes.reasoning: Obscuration {obscuration_pct_per_m:.2f}%/m, alarm level {alarm_level} (Fire 1 or higher).
steps: Send someone to investigate the zone now.
Find the source with a thermal camera.
Isolate power to the affected equipment.
Be ready for suppression release; evacuate if Fire 2.

modes.title: Early smoke warning
modes.cause: Very early sign of particles in the air, before a visible fire.
modes.reasoning: Obscuration {obscuration_pct_per_m:.3f}%/m (alert level).
steps: Walk the zone and look for hot or smelling equipment.
Check for dust from recent work.

modes.title: Suppression agent pressure low
modes.cause: The clean-agent cylinders are losing pressure, so a fire might not be put out.
modes.reasoning: Agent at {agent_pressure_pct:.0f}% of rated pressure (refill below 90%).
steps: Call the fire protection contractor to inspect and refill.
Put a fire watch in place until fixed.

modes.title: Suppression system not armed
modes.cause: The suppression panel is disarmed or in fault (often left disabled after maintenance).
modes.reasoning: Panel armed: {armed}.
steps: Check who disabled it and why.
Re-arm the panel and test.

modes.title: Door forced or held open
modes.cause: A secured door was opened without a valid badge or wedged open.
modes.reasoning: Door forced open; held open {door_held_open_s:.0f} s.
steps: Send security to the door and check the camera.
Confirm who is in the hall.
Repair the door closer or lock.

modes.title: Repeated badge failures
modes.cause: Many failed badge attempts: a broken reader, or someone trying cards.
modes.reasoning: {badge_failures_per_min:.0f} failed badge reads a minute.
steps: Check the camera at the door.
Test the reader with a known-good badge.
